11459.name: Email Collection
11459.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Email Collection, identified as T1114, is a Collection tactic technique used to gather sensitive information from user email. Adversaries target email data on mail servers or clients, including locally stored Outlook files like .ost and .pst, or remotely via services like Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace using credentials or tools such as MailSniper. Groups like Silent Librarian, Scattered Spider, and Magic Hound have employed this method to acquire trade secrets and operational details.
11459.profile_without_enhance_5_without_retriv: [profile]Email Collection is a technique where adversaries gather email data from compromised systems, often leveraging vulnerabilities like CVE-2024-42009 to gain access. The technical mechanics involve extracting email files, archives, or credentials from local mail clients or servers to obtain sensitive communication content for intelligence or further exploitation.[/profile]
11459.profile_without_enhance_5_without_profil: [profile]Email Collection, identified as T1114 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework under the Collection tactic, involves adversaries targeting user email to acquire sensitive information such as trade secrets, personal data, or incident response details. This technique can be executed by collecting or forwarding emails directly from mail servers or clients. A specific vulnerability, CVE-2024-42009, is directly associated with this attack pattern.
11459.profile_without_enhance_5_no_hsage: [profile]Email Collection, designated as T1114 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a collection technique within the Collection tactic that targets email systems across multiple platforms to acquire sensitive data. Adversaries execute this by directly accessing and collecting emails from mail servers or clients, such as Microsoft Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace, often using compromised credentials or tools like MailSniper. The technique can involve parsing local Outlook data files (.ost or .pst) or interacting with remote services, and it is frequently employed by groups like Silent Librarian, Scattered Spider, and Magic Hound to gather intelligence or operational details.

11462.name: Component Object Model Hijacking
11462.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Component Object Model Hijacking is a persistence technique, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1546.015, under the Privilege Escalation tactic for Windows. It works by adversaries modifying Windows Registry entries to replace legitimate COM object references with malicious code, which is then executed in place of the legitimate component during normal system operation. A variation involves hijacking Type Libraries (TypeLibs) to redirect functionality to remote scripts using the "script:" moniker.
11462.profile_without_enhance_5_without_retriv: [profile]Component Object Model Hijacking is a persistence technique where adversaries abuse the Windows Component Object Model (COM) system by hijacking or replacing legitimate COM object references in the registry. This allows malicious code to be executed when the associated legitimate application or system process is invoked, often by modifying registry keys like `HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID` or `HKLM\Software\Classes\CLSID` to point to a malicious payload. The technique facilitates stealthy execution within the context of trusted processes.]
11462.profile_without_enhance_5_without_profil: [profile]Component Object Model Hijacking is a persistence technique (T1546.015) within the Persistence tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It involves adversaries modifying Windows Registry references to legitimate COM objects, redirecting them to malicious code. When the hijacked system component is executed during normal operation, the adversary's payload runs instead. Attackers typically target frequently used COM objects to maintain stealth and avoid system instability. A variation abuses Type Libraries (TypeLibs) to redirect functionality, potentially using the "script:" moniker to execute remote payloads from external servers.

11473.name: Amadey - S1025
11473.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Amadey (also known as Amadey - S1025) is a Trojan bot used since at least 2018, associated with groups like TA505 and Kimsuky. Its key behaviors include using command line options for installation and persistence, injecting a proxy bot into memory, and leveraging techniques like Code Signing, User Execution via phishing, Query Registry for discovery, and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for execution. It primarily targets Windows systems and has been delivered via malicious links to infrastructure in Ukraine.[/profile]
11473.profile_without_enhance_5_without_retriv: [profile]Amadey - S1025, also known as Amadey, is a malware attributed to the UAC-0149 threat actor group. It employs techniques including User Execution via phishing, Code Signing for defense evasion, and Windows Management Instrumentation for execution. It queries the Windows Registry for system discovery. Its target platform is Windows, and it has been observed using infrastructure such as 'https://citactica.com/wp-content/wp-login.php' and 'http://vitantgroup.com/xmlrpc.php' for command and control, with a primary geographic focus on Ukraine.[/profile]
11473.profile_without_enhance_5_without_profil: [profile]Amadey, also known as Amadey - S1025, is a Trojan bot associated with groups like TA505 and Kimsuky. It employs techniques such as Code Signing, User Execution, Query Registry, Phishing, and Windows Management Instrumentation. The malware uses a loader component that can install and start itself with command-line options, and it has been observed targeting systems in Ukraine, utilizing infrastructure like compromised WordPress directories for command and control (e.g., hospitalvilleroy.com.br, vitantgroup.com).]
11473.profile_without_enhance_5_no_hsage: [profile]Amadey, also known as Amadey - S1025, is a Trojan bot used by groups including TA505 and Kimsuky. It functions as a loader that installs itself for persistence and injects a proxy bot into memory, accepting command-line options like /chk, -i, and -s. Its behaviors include OS Credential Dumping, System Network Configuration Discovery, and Remote System Discovery, and it leverages External Remote Services for access. It has targeted Ukraine, with indicators including C2 domains like vitantgroup.com/xmlrpc.php and okesense.oketheme.com.[/profile]
11473.profile_without_enhance_5_no_hsage_no_pr: [profile]Amadey, also known as Amadey Bot, is a Trojan bot used since at least 2018. It has been attributed to threat groups including TA505 and Kimsuky. 16521.name: T1055.013
16521.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055.013, known as Process Doppelgänging, is a sub-technique of Process Injection (T1055) within the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It abuses the deprecated Windows Transactional NTFS (TxF) API to execute arbitrary code in a live process's address space without writing malicious files to disk. The technique operates in four steps: creating a TxF transaction with a legitimate executable and overwriting it with malicious code, loading that code into a shared memory section, rolling back the transaction to remove the file system changes, and finally creating a process from the tainted memory to initiate execution. This method evades process-based defenses by avoiding monitored APIs like NtUnmapViewOfSection and masks execution under a legitimate process, though it typically inherits the injecting process's security context without elevating privileges.

It exploits routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) by using different domain names in the TLS header's SNI field and the HTTP header's Host field; if both domains are hosted on the same CDN, traffic is routed to the domain in the HTTP header, obfuscating the true destination. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation checks.
22251.profile_without_enhance_5_without_retriv: [profile]Domain Fronting is a command-and-control technique where an attacker leverages content delivery networks (CDNs) and other trusted domains to hide the true destination of malicious traffic. By using the fronting domain in the TLS/SSL handshake and the actual malicious domain in the HTTP Host header, the traffic appears to originate from the trusted service, evading network-based detection and filtering. It is applicable across platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS.

It operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. The technique exploits Content Delivery Network (CDN) routing by placing one domain in the TLS header's Server Name Indication (SNI) field and a different, intended destination domain in the HTTP Host header; if both domains are hosted on the same CDN, traffic is routed to the host specified in the HTTP header, obfuscating the true endpoint. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation checks.

The core technical mechanic involves placing one benign domain (e.g., domain-x) in the TLS header's SNI field and a different, actual command-and-control domain (domain-y) in the HTTP Host header; if both domains are hosted on the same CDN, traffic is routed to the hidden domain-y. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation checks. This obfuscates the true destination of HTTPS or tunneled traffic.

23824.name:
This artifact is a cross platform full featured FRP that is written in GO language (Golang) and packed using Ultimate Packer for Executables (UPX). This utility can be used to locate servers behind a network firewall or obscured through NAT. It includes the KCP (no acronym) network protocol that allows for error-checked and anonymous delivery of data streams using the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) with packet level encryption support.

The program contains two different multiplexer libraries that can bi-directionally stream data over a NAT’d network. It also contains a command line interface (CLI) library that can leverage command shells such as PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), and Z Shell (zsh). In addition, the utility features a unique capability that detects if the utility is executed from the command line or by double-clicking. 

By default it is configured to connect to the Internet Protocol (IP) address, 203.95.8.98 on Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) port 1080. It must receive a specially formed packet from the C2 for the utility to deploy on the system.
